planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into the fastest-draining soil available, a raised bed or grit-amended mix; heat tolerance does not offset intolerance of wet feet.

directions: A Ball and Danziger-bred Spanish lavender selection marketed specifically for heat and humidity tolerance in the Gulf Coast and Southeast, with a mounded, self-branching habit that suits borders and containers where looser-habit lavenders rot in summer humidity. Expect a strong spring flush of brightly colored flower wings atop each spike plus a secondary autumn bloom. Give it the sharpest drainage available rather than relying on heat tolerance alone to carry it through a humid summer.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; site where winter flowering in mild Deep South climates won't be hidden.

directions: Billed by its breeder as having among the best heat tolerance of any Spanish lavender, explicitly noted to thrive in hot, humid Texas and Gulf conditions where English lavenders fail. In the Deep South it can bloom nearly year-round, flowering through mild winters rather than going fully dormant. Deadhead spent spikes to extend the bloom flush into fall.

planting.note: Sow onto a moist surface under light 8 weeks before last frost; germination is slow and erratic, so bottom-water and be patient for 2-12 weeks before emergence.

directions: A true seed-propagated Spanish lavender, useful where growers want to raise a heat-tolerant lavender from seed rather than cuttings. It has a compact, rounded habit with classic pinecone-shaped dark purple bloom spikes about 4-5 inches long. Grown as a perennial in zones 8-10 or as a warm-season annual farther north.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; prune after each bloom flush to maintain a tight, non-woody shape.

directions: French lavender is one of the few lavenders that tolerates near-continuous warm-season bloom and genuinely handles Gulf Coast humidity better than English types; this named selection adds creamy-white leaf margins for year-round interest beyond the bloom season. Named for the founder of The Herb Companion magazine. Prune after each bloom flush, since dentata types get leggy fast in a long growing season.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery transplants after last frost into average, well-drained garden soil in full to part sun; full sun intensifies the chartreuse foliage color without scorching.

directions: A Walters Gardens hybrid patented explicitly for blooming through the heat and stress of summer without declining, chosen primarily as a chartreuse-foliage landscape filler rather than a culinary herb. Its leaves are technically edible but it is bred and marketed for ornamental fill and edging, not kitchen use. Full sun brings out the brightest foliage color.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery transplants after last frost into well-drained garden soil in full sun; the chartreuse-yellow foliage resists burning even in intense sun.

directions: A true Origanum vulgare cultivar, so the leaves are edible with a milder flavor than culinary Greek oregano, patented specifically for chartreuse-yellow foliage that resists burning when planted in full sun. Mauve-pink late-summer flowers appear over purple calyxes on a dense, rounded habit. A good choice for southern gardeners wanting a foliage oregano that won't bleach out in intense sun.
